title: Douglas DC-3
description: Airliner and military transport aircraft family
wiki_lead:
The Douglas DC-3 is a propeller-driven airliner that was manufactured by the Douglas Aircraft Company. It had a lasting effect on the airline industry from the 1930s through World War II.
It was developed as a larger, improved, 14-bed sleeper version of the Douglas DC-2.
It is a low-wing metal monoplane with conventional landing gear, powered by two radial piston engines of 1,000–1,200 hp (750–890 kW). Although the DC-3s originally built for civil service had the Wright R-1820 Cyclone, later civilian DC-3s used the Pratt & Whitney R-1830 Twin Wasp engine.
The DC-3 has a cruising speed of 207 mph (333 km/h), a capacity of 21 to 32 passengers or 6,000 lb (2,700 kg) of cargo, and a range of 1,500 mi (2,400 km); it can operate from short runways.
The DC-3 had many exceptional qualities compared to previous aircraft. It was fast, had a good range, was more reliable, and carried passengers in greater comfort. Before World War II, it pioneered many air travel routes. It was able to cross the continental United States from New York to Los Angeles in 18 hours, with only three stops.
It is one of the first airliners that could profitably carry only passengers without relying on mail subsidies. In 1939, at the peak of its dominance in the airliner market, around 90% of airline flights on the planet were by a DC-3 or one of its variants.
Following the war, the airliner market was flooded with surplus transport aircraft, and the DC-3 was no longer competitive because it was smaller and slower than aircraft built during the war. It was made obsolete on main routes by more advanced types such as the Douglas DC-4 and Convair 240, but the design proved adaptable and was still useful on less commercially demanding routes.
Civilian DC-3 production ended in 1943 at 607 aircraft. Military versions, including the C-47 Skytrain (the Dakota in British RAF service), and Soviet- and Japanese-built versions, brought total production to over 16,000.
Many continued to be used in a variety of niche roles; 2,000 DC-3s and military derivatives were estimated to be still flying in 2013; by 2017 more than 300 were still flying. As of 2023, it was estimated about 150 were still flying.

Design and development

"DC" stands for Douglas Commercial. The DC-3 was the culmination of a development effort that began after an inquiry from Transcontinental and Western Airlines (TWA) to Donald Douglas. TWA's rival in transcontinental air service, United Airlines, was starting service with the Boeing 247, and Boeing refused to sell any 247s to other airlines until United's order for 60 aircraft had been filled. TWA asked Douglas to design and build an aircraft that would allow TWA to compete with United. Douglas' design, the 1933 DC-1, was promising, and led to the DC-2 in 1934. The DC-2 was a success, but with room for improvement.

grok_lead: The Douglas DC-3 is a twin-engine propeller-driven airliner developed by the Douglas Aircraft Company in the 1930s, renowned for its role in revolutionizing commercial aviation by enabling profitable passenger transport without government subsidies. First flown on December 17, 1935, as an enlarged variant of the DC-2, it featured a capacity for 21 passengers, a cruising speed of approximately 200 mph (322 km/h), and a range of up to 1,500 miles (2,414 km), powered by two 1,200-horsepower radial engines such as the Wright Cyclone or Pratt & Whitney Twin Wasp. With dimensions including a 95-foot (29 m) wingspan, 64-foot-6-inch (19.7 m) length, and maximum takeoff weight of 25,200 pounds (11,431 kg), the DC-3 offered enhanced reliability, safety, and comfort compared to predecessors, including options for sleeper berths in its DST variant. 607 civil versions were produced, alongside more than 10,000 military variants like the C-47 Skytrain, which played a pivotal role in World War II operations, including troop and cargo transport. The DC-3's development stemmed from the need to address the limitations of earlier airliners, evolving directly from the DC-2, which had increased passenger capacity to 14 and improved performance over the prototype DC-1 that first flew in 1933. Key figures included Donald W. Douglas, the company founder, and chief engineer Arthur E. Raymond, who incorporated innovations like retractable landing gear, NACA engine cowlings, and a multi-spar wing design for better structural integrity and efficiency. Prompted by a 1934 request from American Airlines president C.R. Smith for a more spacious and economical aircraft, the DC-3 entered commercial service on June 25, 1936, quickly becoming the backbone of U.S. airline s and serving 90% of the world's carriers by 1939. Its all-metal construction, conventional tailwheel landing gear, and ability to operate from shorter runways made it versatile for both domestic and international routes, carrying over 2 million passengers annually by the late 1930s and shifting airline economics from mail subsidies to passenger revenue. Militarily, the DC-3 was adapted as the C-47 Skytrain (or Dakota in British service), with over 10,000 units built for the U.S. Army Air Forces and Allies, facilitating critical logistics such as the D-Day invasion paratroop drops and supply chains across theaters. Post-World War II, surplus military models flooded the civilian market, sustaining the type's use in passenger, cargo, and specialized roles worldwide, with some aircraft accumulating over 50,000 flight hours. The DC-3's enduring legacy lies in its influence on modern air travel, demonstrating that safe, efficient, and comfortable flight could be commercially viable, and as of 2025, hundreds remain airworthy for bush operations, firefighting, and heritage flights, underscoring its timeless design.
